summary: Describes the IS-IS extensions needed for Segment Routing running on an MPLS data plane. IS-IS advertises the segments that let flexible end-to-end paths be built as sequences of topological subpaths.

eli5.summary: IS-IS is another way routers share maps. This adds the extra signposts so a path can be assembled from pieces.

questions: what is a prefix sid in is-is
what is the sid label binding tlv
subtitle: How IS-IS routers advertise the identifiers and label ranges that Segment Routing over MPLS relies on.

tldr.problem: Segment Routing builds paths from segments, so every router needs a way to tell the others which segment identifiers it has and which MPLS label ranges it uses.
tldr.mechanism: IS-IS gets new sub-TLVs for Prefix-SIDs, Adjacency SIDs and LAN Adjacency SIDs, two new Binding TLVs for mapping prefixes to SIDs, and new Router Capability sub-TLVs for label ranges and algorithms.
tldr.outcome: SR paths over MPLS then need no LDP or RSVP-TE signaling, only the regular IGP. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 8667 is a Proposed Standard, published in December 2019, and has not been obsoleted or updated. The OSPF equivalent is RFC 8665.

sections.title: Segment Routing in IS-IS
sections.content:
Segment Routing (SR) encodes an end-to-end path as a sequence of topological subpaths called segments, and the link-state protocols advertise them. A prefix segment is an ECMP-aware shortest path to a prefix or node. An adjacency segment is a hop over one specific adjacency.

SR can use IPv6 or MPLS data planes and needs no signaling beyond the regular IGP. With MPLS, SR paths need no LDP or RSVP-TE, but can interoperate with LSPs those protocols set up. This document covers IS-IS for an MPLS data plane. It also defines an advertisement for one Binding SID type, the Mirror Context segment. The architecture is in RFC 8402; the OSPF counterpart is RFC 8665.
sections.eli5: A long trip is cut into short pieces, and each piece gets a name tag. IS-IS is taught to pass those tags around.

sections.title: The Prefix-SID Sub-TLV
sections.content:
The Prefix-SID sub-TLV (Type 3) carries the IGP-Prefix-SID for a prefix. It may appear in TLV 135, 235, 236 and 237 (extended IPv4, multi-topology IPv4, IPv6 and multi-topology IPv6 reachability). Without the L-Flag, the Prefix-SID MUST be unique within the IGP domain. Length is 5 or 6 depending on the SID size.

  • R: the prefix was propagated between levels or redistributed.
  • N: Node-SID, for a prefix on a local interface with length /32 (IPv4) or /128 (IPv6).
  • P: no penultimate hop popping.
  • E: Explicit NULL (0 for IPv4 and 2 for IPv6).
  • V and L: value instead of index, and local significance.

The Algorithm field MUST be 0 or a value the router advertised in its SR-Algorithm sub-TLV. A receiver MUST ignore a Prefix-SID whose algorithm the originator never advertised.

The V/L combinations that are valid are both 0 (a 4-octet index into the router's advertised label space) and both 1 (a 3-octet local label, 20 rightmost bits). Anything else MUST be ignored.

If P is clear, upstream neighbors MUST pop the SID. If P is set and E clear, they keep it on top of the stack, which suits a border router stitching into a continuing LSP. If both are set, they swap it for Explicit NULL. When a router propagates a prefix between Level-1 and Level-2, it MUST set P and clear E. The Prefix-SID sub-TLV MUST be included when the prefix is propagated across levels.
sections.eli5: A Prefix-SID is a name tag for a place. Little switches on the tag say whether the second-to-last stop should take it off, and whether the tag names a whole router or just one address.

sections.title: Adjacency and LAN Adjacency SIDs
sections.content:
The Adj-SID sub-TLV (Type 31) names a single IS-IS adjacency. It goes inside the neighbor TLVs 22, 23, 141, 222 and 223. Flags are F (IPv4 when unset, IPv6 when set), B (eligible for fast-reroute protection), V (default set), L (default set), S (refers to a set of adjacencies) and P (persistent). It also has a one-octet Weight used for load balancing. A router MAY allocate an Adj-SID per adjacency, several for one adjacency, or one shared across adjacencies. When P is set, the Adj-SID MUST be persistent.

On a LAN, the elected Designated Intermediate System (DIS) originates the Pseudonode LSP, and each router advertises only one adjacency, to the DIS. So each router lists the Adj-SIDs of its LAN neighbors in LAN-Adj-SID sub-TLVs (Type 32), each with the neighbor's System-ID. This sub-TLV MUST NOT appear in TLV 141. If one advertisement cannot hold them all, several advertisements with the same metric MUST be used.
sections.eli5: An Adj-SID is a tag for one step between two neighbors. On a shared street, each house keeps a list of tags for the neighbors it can step to.

sections.title: SID/Label Binding TLVs and the Mapping Server
sections.content:
The SID/Label Binding TLV (Type 149) may be originated by any router. It lets a Segment Routing Mapping Server attach SIDs to prefixes, and can advertise a Mirror SID for a node that can process traffic meant for another node. Fields are Flags, a 2-octet Range, a Prefix Length and the Prefix, followed by sub-TLVs.

  • F: IPv4 when unset, IPv6 when set.
  • M: mirror context.
  • S: flood across the whole routing domain; if unset the TLV MUST NOT be leaked between levels.
  • D: MUST be set when leaked from Level-2 to Level-1, and such TLVs MUST NOT be leaked back up.
  • A: the prefix is directly attached to the originator.

The Range compresses a run of consecutive prefixes onto consecutive SIDs, with the prefix being the first address. A single SID uses Range 1. The RFC gives an example of four loopbacks, 192.0.2.1 to 192.0.2.4, mapped to indexes 1 to 4 with Range 4. When the M-Flag is clear, a Prefix-SID sub-TLV MUST be present; when set, it MUST NOT be. Mappings that are not continuous need several Binding TLVs.

The Multi-Topology SID/Label Binding TLV (Type 150) has the same format with a 12-bit MT ID added. It MUST be ignored if the ID is zero.
sections.eli5: A binding says 'these ten houses in a row get these ten tags in a row', so one note covers a whole street.

sections.title: Router Capabilities
sections.content:
Capabilities ride in the IS-IS Router Capability TLV from RFC 7981. They are propagated throughout a level and MUST NOT cross level boundaries, so the S-Flag in the Router Capability TLV MUST be unset.

  • SR-Capabilities (Type 2): flags I (can process SR-MPLS IPv4) and V (IPv6), then one or more SRGB descriptors, each a 3-octet Range greater than 0 and a SID/Label sub-TLV with the first label. A router MUST NOT advertise more than one.
  • SR-Algorithm (Type 19): lists algorithms. Algorithm 0 is metric-based SPF, which a node may override by local policy. Algorithm 1 is Strict SPF, which local policy MUST NOT alter. If it is absent, only algorithm 0 is supported. If present, algorithm 0 MUST be included.
  • SR Local Block (Type 22): labels reserved for local SIDs such as Adj-SIDs, in the same descriptor format. No flags are defined.
  • SRMS Preference (Type 24): a one-octet unsigned preference for mapping server advertisements.

Order matters. When several SRGB ranges are advertised, a SID index is applied across them in order, and the RFC's example concatenates ranges starting at 100, 1000 and 500, each of size 100, so index 100 means label 1000. Reordering ranges causes label churn and may black-hole or misdirect traffic, so new blocks SHOULD be added at the end and the order MUST survive a graceful restart. Ranges MUST NOT overlap.
sections.eli5: Each router announces which kinds of route-finding it knows and which block of numbers it uses for tags. The order of the blocks matters, so changing it would confuse everyone.

sections.title: Registrations
sections.content:
IANA allocated Adjacency Segment Identifier (31) and LAN Adjacency Segment Identifier (32) sub-TLVs for TLVs 22, 23, 141, 222 and 223, and Prefix Segment Identifier (3) for TLVs 135, 235, 236 and 237. In the Router Capability TLV (242) it allocated sub-TLVs 2, 19, 22 and 24.

New TLVs 149 (Segment Identifier / Label Binding) and 150 (Multi-Topology Segment Identifier / Label Binding) are valid in LSPs only. A new registry, Sub-TLVs for TLVs 149 and 150, uses Expert Review and starts with 1 (SID/Label) and 3 (Prefix Segment Identifier).
sections.eli5: Numbers were reserved in the official list so that nobody else uses the same number for something different.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: IS-IS now carries information used to program the MPLS data plane. The same kinds of attacks possible on the IP or IPv6 control plane can be carried out on the MPLS control plane and misroute traffic, and may be harder to detect and isolate. The existing IS-IS authentication of RFC 5304 and RFC 5310 applies to these extensions. The RFC adds no new security mechanism.
sections.eli5: Since these tags now steer real traffic, a fake one could send it the wrong way. The routers keep using the checks IS-IS already has.

fields.desc: Index, or local label, depending on V and L.
